title: Max your IRA — Roth, Traditional, or Backdoor
summary: Same $7,500 limit. Same bracket-based logic as W-2.
detailsHtml:
IRA limits don't differ for contractors. The bracket-sensitive decision is identical to the W-2 path.

${bracketBlock( 'Roth IRA, direct contribution. Your bracket is low enough that paying tax now is almost certainly correct.', 'Roth or Traditional based on retirement projection. Hedge by splitting if uncertain.', 'Backdoor Roth IRA almost certainly required. Caution: if you have a SEP-IRA or SIMPLE IRA balance, the pro-rata rule will tax most of your conversion. Consider rolling SEP/SIMPLE balances into a Solo 401(k) first to clear the IRA balance, then execute the backdoor Roth cleanly. This is a common contractor-specific complication.' )}
Pro-rata rule pitfall: The backdoor Roth's pro-rata calculation aggregates all Traditional IRA balances (including SEP-IRA and SIMPLE IRA) on December 31 of the conversion year. Three exclusions worth knowing: (1) inherited IRAs are excluded under §408(d)(3)(C); (2) Roth IRA balances are not aggregated — only pre-tax IRAs; (3) 401(k) and Solo 401(k) balances are not aggregated, which is why the standard fix is rolling SEP/SIMPLE/Traditional IRA balances into a 401(k) before December 31. One catch: SIMPLE IRA balances cannot be rolled to a 401(k) for 2 years after first participation per IRC §72(t)(6). A contractor with a SIMPLE balance under 2 years old has no clean fix and should defer the backdoor Roth until the 2-year clock runs.
